live.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
live.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT: a threat actor known by many names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists NICKEL FOXCROFT under many aliases, including APT37 and ScarCruft, and names eight tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL FOXCROFT is the Secureworks name for a threat actor tracked under many other names.
Its aliases include APT37, ATK4, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Operation Daybreak, Operaton Erebus, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA, Reaper, ScarCruft, TA-RedAnt and Venus 121.
The catalogue links eight tools to the actor: Bluelight, Chinotto, GOLDBACKDOOR, KevDroid, KoSpy, PoorWeb, ROKRAT and final1stpy.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
next.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT (APT37): a long-running espionage actor focused on Korean targets
next.in_short: NICKEL FOXCROFT, also tracked as APT37 and ScarCruft, is described by several vendors as a North Korea-aligned espionage group. It favours phishing, cloud-based command channels and custom backdoors such as ROKRAT.

sentences.t: The catalogue tracks NICKEL FOXCROFT under many names, including APT37, ScarCruft, Reaper, InkySquid, Group 123 and RICOCHET CHOLLIMA.
CrowdStrike describes RICOCHET CHOLLIMA as a DPRK-nexus targeted intrusion adversary that has run espionage operations since at least 2016.
Lookout describes ScarCruft as a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage group active since 2012.
ESET says ScarCruft is suspected to be a North Korean espionage group and has operated since at least 2012.
One researcher writes that the group's exact relationship with the North Korean state remains somewhat unclear, and that coordination by the government is believed rather than confirmed.
Genians notes that some researchers class KONNI, Kimsuky and APT37 as one group, because their targets and infrastructure overlap. Other sources treat them as distinct.
CrowdStrike says observed operations have almost exclusively targeted the Republic of Korea. It assesses they focus on government officials, NGOs, academics and journalists.
AhnLab's ASEC says the group targets individuals such as human rights activists, reporters and North Korean defectors.
Genians reports a March 2025 spear phishing campaign, attributed to APT37, aimed at activists focused on North Korea.
ESET infers that a game-platform attack mainly targeted ethnic Koreans in Yanbian, China, most likely refugees or defectors.
360 Advanced Threat Research Institute says a campaign by this actor targeted government personnel and corporations in South Korea and Asia.
One analysis describes phishing emails with ZIP files that hide LNK shortcuts. These run a multi-stage script chain that loads the ROKRAT backdoor in memory.
ROKRAT uses legitimate cloud services such as pCloud, Yandex and Dropbox for command and control.
360 says RokRat has been the group's primary remote access tool since 2016.
ASEC reports an attack on a flaw in the Hangul word processor (CVE-2017-8291). It hid its payload in a JPEG image and installed a new backdoor called M2RAT.
Zscaler describes chains that drop the Rust backdoor Rustonotto, the PowerShell backdoor Chinotto and the data-theft tool FadeStealer.
Zscaler's Ruby Jumper report describes spreading over removable media to reach air-gapped networks. To its knowledge, it was the first time APT37 had abused Zoho WorkDrive.
The catalogue lists the group's tools as including Bluelight, Chinotto, GOLDBACKDOOR, KevDroid, KoSpy, PoorWeb, ROKRAT and final1stpy.

S2W analysed a December 2020 watering-hole attack that delivered a ROKRAT variant. From the techniques used, it judged the activity related to ScarCruft. That is a judgement, not a confirmed attribution.
Lookout attributes the KoSpy Android spyware to APT37 with medium confidence. The samples date from March 2022 to March 2024.
ESET reports that ScarCruft trojanized Windows and Android parts of a video game platform for Yanbian. The attack was probably ongoing since late 2024.
Genians named its March 2025 campaign Operation ToyBox Story. Lures posed as a South Korean national security think tank, and the final payload was RoKRAT.
Treat unexpected shortcut files, archives and document attachments with suspicion, especially when they claim to come from a think tank or an event organiser.
Monitor for script activity and unusual traffic to cloud storage services.
